claims.text: High configurational entropy theoretically favors stabilization of a single-phase solid solution in multielement alloys.
High mixing entropy alone is insufficient to guarantee that five-transition-metal HENA nanoparticles remain single phase at elevated temperature.
Five-metal HENA materials may undergo dissolution despite their high configurational entropy.
Long-term structural stability is governed by a sluggish-diffusion kinetic barrier that delays grain growth and elemental segregation.
Diffusion coefficients in these HENAs are approximately 10^-19 m²/s and three orders of magnitude below those in traditional binary alloys.
Thermally stable secondary phases such as Laves phases or B2 precipitates form in the alloy.
Secondary phases pin grain boundaries and inhibit further grain growth.
During the initial annealing stage, sluggish diffusion suppresses mass transport and preserves the single-phase state.
After 10–100 hours, local concentration fluctuations produce non-monotonic chemical changes and transient phase reconstruction through spinodal decomposition or precipitation.
Equimolar PtRuIrRhPd nanoparticles can be synthesized by carbothermal shock.
High-energy synthesis produces a single-phase five-metal solid solution with high lattice distortion.
TiCoCrFeMn is an example of the proposed initially single-phase HENA nanoparticle state.
The material exhibits rapid grain growth or phase fluctuation during the first 10–50 hours of annealing.
Grain-growth kinetics slow substantially and structural stabilization occurs after approximately 100 hours at 1000 °C.
A matrix-plus-precipitate two-phase microstructure persists through 1000 hours of annealing.
Traditional alloying concepts predict that equiatomic composition maximizes entropy and therefore stability.
Traditional alloying concepts predict monotonic grain growth without phase separation.
A constituent with a substantially lower melting point or greater volatility can invalidate the sluggish-diffusion stability regime.
A highly negative mixing enthalpy can favor immediate intermetallic formation instead of a sluggish-diffusion regime.
Below a critical nanoparticle size, surface energy can dominate bulk diffusion barriers and invalidate the proposed model.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says sluggish diffusion delays the onset of grain growth until a critical threshold, whereas the predicted outcome specifies rapid grain growth during the initial 10–50 hours.
The stated conditions restrict annealing times to greater than 100 hours, but the intervention and predicted outcome require observations between 10 and 50 hours.
